notes: Slot 4 = Communist Party of Azerbaijan under Aliyev (First Secretary since July 1969). Müsavat in exile in 1 (follows MD). Aliyev's KGB network as catchy power bloc in 7, Akhundov's purged old guard in 6, Aliyev's Nakhchivan patronage in 13 (MD puts Aliyev's YAP there). Pishevari's exiled Azerbaijan Democratic Party (Firqa, Baku) in 18; Mustafayev-style national communists in 19. Baku Spiritual Board in 8 (Shia-led). No MD sprite shows a 1970 organization, so icons null.

0.name: Azerbaycan Kültür Derneği
0.text:
The Azerbaijan Cultural Association is the main organisation of the Azerbaijani emigration in Turkey, founded in Ankara in 1949 by Mammad Amin Rasulzade, leader of the short-lived Azerbaijan Democratic Republic of 1918–1920. Since his death in 1955 it has been run by veteran émigrés who publish the journal Azerbaycan and cultivate ties with the Turkish state and its security establishment.

It calls for an independent, anti-communist Azerbaijan under a strong national government allied with Turkey and the West. Its members advise Turkish officials, contribute to Radio Liberty and keep the tricolour of 1918 alive. Inside the Soviet republic its voice reaches only shortwave listeners, but it guards the memory of national statehood.

1.name: Müsavat Partiyası
1.text:
The Müsavat Party, founded in Baku in 1911, led the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic until the Red Army's invasion of April 1920. Destroyed at home, it survives in Turkish exile as a small émigré party carrying the legacy of its leader Mammad Amin Rasulzade, who died in Ankara in 1955.

Its programme is national democracy: an independent, secular Azerbaijani republic with a parliament, private property and close ties to Turkey and the West. Inside the Soviet republic the name Müsavat is a political curse, invoked by propaganda against 'bourgeois nationalists'. Its leverage lies in family memories of 1918, in Turkey's protection and in the slow rediscovery of national history among Baku students.

2.name: Azärbaycan Yazıçılar İttifaqı
2.text:
The Union of Writers of Azerbaijan is the official association of the republic's authors and the most prestigious forum of the Azerbaijani intelligentsia. Beside senior figures such as the novelist Mirza Ibrahimov stand poets and prose writers like Rasul Rza, Bakhtiyar Vahabzade, Anar and Elchin, whose works test the limits of censorship with modernist forms and national themes.

The writers press for wider use of Azerbaijani in schools and offices, freer debate on history and gentler censorship, while proclaiming loyalty to Soviet power. Vahabzade's poem Gülüstan, lamenting the 1813 treaty that divided Azerbaijan, earned him party reprimands. Their leverage lies in a mass readership and the party's need for respected national voices.

3.name: Azärbaycan Hämkarlar İttifaqları Şurası
3.text:
The Azerbaijan Trade Union Council is the republican body of the Soviet trade unions, organising Baku's oil workers, refinery hands, textile operatives and builders. It inherits the memory of the great Baku oil strikes of 1904 and 1914 and officially serves as a 'school of communism' under party supervision.

Within its committees a pragmatic, welfare-minded current presses for housing, wages, pensions and safety on the ageing Absheron oilfields and the offshore platforms of Neft Daşları. It favours consultation with workers over mobilisation campaigns and fair distribution over prestige projects. Its leverage lies in the oil workers, whose output the Union still needs, and in control of sanatoriums, holidays and housing queues.

4.name: Azärbaycan Kommunist Partiyası
4.text:
The Communist Party of Azerbaijan is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Azerbaijan SSR. In July 1969 Moscow replaced the long-serving Veli Akhundov with Heydar Aliyev, the 46-year-old chairman of the republic's KGB, as First Secretary.

Aliyev has opened a loud campaign against corruption, bribery and the sale of posts, purging Akhundov's appointees and placing trusted colleagues in key jobs. The party promotes oil, cotton, viticulture and industrial growth, Soviet patriotism and a carefully controlled Azerbaijani identity. Its power rests on the nomenklatura, the security organs and Aliyev's rapidly growing standing with Leonid Brezhnev.

5.name: Azärbaycan Lenin Kommunist Gänclär İttifaqı
5.english: Leninist Young Communist League of Azerbaijan
5.text:
The Leninist Young Communist League of Azerbaijan is the republic's Komsomol, organising pupils, students and young workers in Baku, Sumgait, Kirovabad and the villages. It staffs construction brigades for the industrial city of Sumgait and the Caspian oil platforms, runs youth clubs and trains the party's next generation of officials.

Its activist core sees itself as the revolutionary guard of Soviet modernity against religion, patriarchal custom, bride abduction and the corruption of the Akhundov years. It champions women's emancipation, atheism and internationalism, and is eager to serve Aliyev's anti-corruption drive. Its leverage lies in mobilisation and in its role as the main ladder into the nomenklatura.

6.name: Köhnä qvardiya
6.text:
The Old Guard is the network of party secretaries, ministers and district bosses who rose under Veli Akhundov, First Secretary from 1959 until his removal in July 1969. Russian-speaking, Moscow-schooled and comfortable with the patronage of the 1960s, they now watch Heydar Aliyev's purges with fear and resentment.

They defend Brezhnev's 'stability of cadres', strict ideological orthodoxy and the primacy of Baku's Russified elite over provincial newcomers. They distrust both national-minded writers and Aliyev's Chekists, and appeal to friends in the Central Committee in Moscow for protection. Their leverage lies in surviving posts, compromising files on rivals and the hope that Aliyev's star will fade.

7.name: Çekistlär
7.text:
The Chekists are the officers of the KGB of the Azerbaijan SSR who served under Heydar Aliyev and now follow him into power. The service is chaired by Ziya Yusifzade, while Aliyev's patron Semyon Tsvigun, head of the Azerbaijani KGB in 1963–1967, is now deputy chairman of the KGB in Moscow.

They believe the republic must be governed by disciplined, incorruptible professionals: informant networks, quiet dossiers and surgical purges rather than ideological campaigns. They monitor émigré links, religious activity, nationalists and black marketeers alike. Their leverage is enormous: files on every official, a direct channel to the Lubyanka and a patron who now runs the republic.

8.name: Zaqafqaziya Müsälmanları Ruhani İdaräsi
8.english: Spiritual Board of the Muslims of Transcaucasia
8.text:
The Spiritual Board of the Muslims of Transcaucasia, seated at Baku's Täzä Pir Mosque, is the officially registered Islamic authority for the Shia and Sunni believers of Azerbaijan, Georgia and Armenia. Headed by a Shia sheikh ul-Islam with a Sunni mufti as deputy, it supervises the handful of mosques the state allows to remain open.

It preaches loyalty to Soviet power, Shia–Sunni harmony and a modern, quiet faith compatible with socialism, and serves Moscow's diplomacy towards Iran and the Arab world. Its clergy are few and closely watched by the Council for Religious Affairs. Its leverage lies in being the only legal voice of a still largely believing Muslim population.

9.name: Närdäran cämaäti
9.text:
The Nardaran Congregation is the conservative Shia milieu of Nardaran and neighbouring villages on the Absheron peninsula, famous for its piety and for the shrine of Rahima Khanum. Unregistered mullahs, self-taught or trained before the revolution, lead prayers, Muharram mourning and forbidden Ashura processions beyond the reach of the official Spiritual Board.

Its believers reject atheist education and Soviet customs and look with reverence to the great Shia clerics of Najaf and Qom. They are not organised politically, but their networks of family, shrine and mosque survive every anti-religious campaign. Their leverage lies in a closed community that the authorities find hard to penetrate.

10.name: Zaqatala alimläri
10.text:
The Scholars of Zaqatala are the Sunni religious teachers of Azerbaijan's north-west, where Avars, Tsakhurs and Azerbaijanis keep a tradition of learning closely tied to Dagestan. Working mostly outside registered mosques, they teach Arabic, Quran recitation and jurisprudence in private homes, sometimes to students who go on to Bukhara.

They preach obedience to authority, strict personal piety and avoidance of politics, and look to the Sunni scholars of Dagestan rather than to Baku's Shia-led Spiritual Board. They ask only for quiet tolerance of religious education. Their leverage lies in their moral authority over the mountain villages of Zaqatala, Balakan and Qakh, where faith and clan remain intertwined.

11.name: Müridlär
11.text:
The Murids are clandestine Naqshbandi disciples in the mountain districts of northern Azerbaijan, heirs of the brotherhood that sustained Imam Shamil's holy war against Russia in the nineteenth century. Their sheikhs, mostly linked to Dagestani masters, initiate followers in secret, and the KGB counts them among the most stubborn forms of 'unofficial Islam'.

They teach that true Islam requires a state governed by sharia under a righteous imam, and that Soviet power, like the Tsarist conquest, is a passing infidel rule. They have neither arms nor structure for revolt, but cultivate discipline, secrecy and the memory of jihad. Their leverage lies in a loyalty that runs deeper than any party card.

12.name: Usrat al-Qiyam
12.text:
The Qiyam Circle is a small group of Algerian students at Baku's Azizbekov Institute of Oil and Chemistry who sympathise with al-Qiyam, the Islamic values society founded in Algiers in 1963 and suppressed by Boumediene's government. Sent to train as engineers for Algeria's oil industry, they pray together and read Muslim Brotherhood literature in secret.

They seek an Islamic social order built through education, morality and preaching, reject atheism and are uneasy with their own government's socialism. They look for contact with Azerbaijani believers, but language and surveillance are hard barriers. Their leverage in Baku is small; their significance lies in the Islamist networks they carry back home.

13.name: Naxçıvan klanı
13.text:
The Nakhchivan Clan is the network of officials from Heydar Aliyev's native Nakhchivan, joined by former KGB colleagues and loyal technocrats, now being placed in key posts across the republic. It is less an ideological faction than a regional patronage system bound by kinship, shared origins and personal loyalty to the new First Secretary.

It values order, results and loyalty over doctrine, and treats Moscow's ideological campaigns as rituals to be performed while real decisions are made among trusted men. It favours large industrial and agricultural projects that can be reported upward as triumphs. Its leverage lies in appointments: whoever controls cadres controls the republic, and the clan increasingly does.

14.name: Ağsaqqallar
14.text:
The Elders are the white-bearded patriarchs of Azerbaijan's villages and old Baku quarters, respected heads of extended families who settle disputes, arrange marriages and mediate between neighbours, kolkhoz chairmen and district officials. In Shirvan, Karabakh, Lankaran and Nakhchivan their word often weighs more than a court ruling.

They stand for family honour, respect for age, modesty of women and quiet observance of Islamic customs such as funerals, circumcision and Novruz, all within a Soviet framework they have learned to live with. They distrust radical modernisers and agitators alike. Their leverage is social: few officials can govern a district without the elders' consent.

15.name: Neft generalları
15.text:
The Oil Generals are the directors of the republic's oil production associations, refineries and petrochemical plants in Baku and Sumgait, together with the managers of the offshore field at Neft Daşları. Once the heart of Soviet oil, the Absheron fields are declining as Siberia rises, but they still command vast budgets and tens of thousands of jobs.

They want investment in deep offshore drilling, modern equipment and freedom from ministerial micromanagement, and quietly tolerate padded reports and side deals with supply bases. Ideologically indifferent, they value production figures, privileges and access to Moscow's ministries. Their leverage lies in the industry's prestige and the resources they can steer to friends.

16.name: Täzä bazar
16.text:
Teze Bazaar, Baku's great market, gives its name to the republic's world of private traders: kolkhoz-market sellers, flower and citrus growers who fly their produce to Moscow and Leningrad, carpet dealers and middlemen of the second economy. Azerbaijani traders are fixtures of markets across the Soviet Union.

They want freedom to grow and sell, fewer checks on private plots and transport, and an end to campaigns against 'speculators', which Aliyev's crackdown threatens to renew. They care little for ideology and much for profit, family and connections. Their leverage lies in cash, in goods the state shops cannot supply and in the many officials whose comfort depends on them.

17.name: Azärbaycan Täbiäti Mühafizä Cämiyyäti
17.text:
The Azerbaijan Society for Nature Conservation is the republic's official voluntary conservation body, uniting biologists, teachers, foresters and schoolchildren under the patronage of the Academy of Sciences. Its specialists know the Caspian shore, the Kura delta and the Hirkan forests of Lankaran better than any ministry.

They warn that oil spills around Absheron, untreated waste from Sumgait's chemical plants and dams on the Kura are destroying fisheries, above all the Caspian sturgeon, and poisoning Baku's air. They work through lectures, scientific reports and proposals for new nature reserves, carefully avoiding open criticism of the plan. Their leverage is scientific and grows with every dead fish washed ashore.

18.name: Azärbaycan Demokrat Firqäsi
18.text:
The Azerbaijan Democratic Party, known simply as the Firqa, was founded in Tabriz in 1945 by Jafar Pishevari and ran the Soviet-backed autonomous government of Iranian Azerbaijan until its collapse in December 1946. Thousands of its members fled north and have lived in Baku ever since; formally merged with the Tudeh Party in 1960, it keeps its own name under Gholam Yahya Daneshian.

It stands for socialism, land reform and national rights for the Azerbaijanis of Iran, and dreams of a return to Tabriz. Loyal to Moscow, it nonetheless keeps alive the idea of one Azerbaijani nation divided by a border. Its leverage lies in its veterans, its émigré press and Soviet interest in pressuring the Shah.

19.name: Narimanovçular
19.text:
Narimanov's Heirs are the national-minded communists of Azerbaijan who invoke Nariman Narimanov, the republic's first Soviet leader, who defended Azerbaijani interests against Moscow's centralism in the early 1920s. Their best-known figure is Imam Mustafayev, First Secretary from 1954 to 1959, removed after the 1956 law making Azerbaijani the state language and now a scientist at the Academy of Sciences.

They seek a socialism rooted in Azerbaijani language and culture: native-language schooling and administration, a fair share of the republic's oil wealth and more Azerbaijani cadres at the top. They remain Marxists loyal to the Union but resent Russification. Their leverage lies among educators, scholars and officials who quietly share their convictions.

20.name: Bütöv Azärbaycan
20.text:
Whole Azerbaijan is the clandestine nationalist milieu of Baku students and young scholars who dream of uniting Soviet Azerbaijan with the Azerbaijani provinces of Iran, divided by the treaties of 1813 and 1828. Among its circles is that of Abulfaz Aliyev, a young Arabist teaching at Azerbaijan State University, and it draws inspiration from the defiant verse of the poet Khalil Rza.

It calls for Azerbaijani as the sole language of public life, a national history free of Russian tutelage and solidarity with the Turkic peoples, edging towards outright independence. Its members meet in flats and study circles and fear informers above all. Its leverage lies in rising national feeling among the young.

21.name: Ülkü Ocakları
21.text:
The Grey Wolves, organised since 1968 as the Idealist Hearths, are the militant youth wing of Alparslan Türkeş's Nationalist Movement Party in Turkey and the spearhead of pan-Turkism. Azerbaijani émigrés in Turkey, among them veterans of the wartime Azerbaijani Legion, find a home in their ranks and press for the liberation of the 'captive Turks' of the USSR.

The movement preaches a mystical Turkish nationalism, the dream of Turan uniting all Turkic peoples, paramilitary discipline and violent anti-communism, and hails Azerbaijan as a stolen Turkic land. Inside the Soviet republic it has no organisation, but its slogans circulate through émigré literature and Turkish radio. Its leverage lies in Turkish street power.

22.name: Bakinskiy okrug PVO
22.text:
The Baku Air Defence District is one of only two air defence districts of the Soviet Union, guarding the Caucasus, the Caspian oilfields and the southern frontier against air attack from Iran and Turkey. Together with the 4th Army and the Caspian Flotilla, both headquartered in Baku, it makes the city one of the most militarised in the Union.

Its officer corps, overwhelmingly Russian and Ukrainian, sees Azerbaijan as a frontline facing NATO's Turkey and the Shah's American-armed Iran. It keeps aloof from republican politics but would act decisively against unrest or nationalist secession. Its leverage lies in airfields, missile sites, garrisons and the strategic weight of the southern border.

23.name: Qacarlar sülaläsi
23.text:
The Qajar dynasty is the Turkic house that ruled Iran and, through its Ziyadoglu branch, the Ganja Khanate, before Russia annexed the khanates of present-day Azerbaijan in 1813–1828. Deposed in Iran in 1925, the family lives in exile; its head, Prince Hamid Mirza, has made his life in Britain.

For a handful of émigré monarchists and old aristocratic families, the Qajars symbolise a Turkic-ruled Islamic realm before Russian and Pahlavi rule. They favour a traditional monarchy respectful of Shia Islam and Turkic heritage, and reject both Soviet power and the Pahlavi state. Their leverage is minimal, resting on lineage, memory and émigré salons in Paris and London.
